Australian English is the accent and dialect of Australia, marked by a distinctive vowel system, non-rhotic pronunciation influenced by British English, and colloquial vocabulary unique to Australia. Though historically stigmatized as inferior compared to British English, it has gained acceptance and become a symbol of Australian identity.

Like Received Pronunciation, Australian English is non-rhotic, meaning the r is silent except before vowels, so "car" is pronounced "cah." The short "i" vowel shifts toward an "e" sound, making "kit" sound like "ket" and "bid" like "bed." One distinctive feature is the rising intonation on statements, making many declarative sentences sound like questions. This is called High Rising Terminal.

Other vowel shifts include "trap" shifting toward "drip" and "strut" toward "sport." Australian English is also known for colloquial vocabulary and diminutives like "servo" for service station, "brekkie" for breakfast, and "arvo" for afternoon.

Rhotic variants do exist in Tasmania and some rural areas, but non-rhotic prestige speech dominates urban centers like Sydney and Melbourne.

Australian English maintains stronger British influence than General American, the major prestige American standard. It is a closely related variety to New Zealand English in the Oceania region, sharing many features with that accent as well.
